## The eight founder-emulation items

1. **Who.** Engineers at AI-native startups keeping an LLM agent working for customers in production.
   [LYC] "Before starting Lemma, we were engineers at two high growth, AI-native startups: Tandem (AI for healthcare) and
   Chipstack (AI agents for chip design)." [LYC] "If you're building with LLMs and run a ton of prompt or eval
   experiments, we'd love for you to work with us." → `roles[engineer]`, `context.actor`, `actor_plural`.

2. **What (the job).** Keep the agent doing what customers need as real traffic changes.
   [LYC] "AI agents don't learn from their mistakes. In fact, they get worse with use." [LYC] "In production, prompts
   and agents continuously degrade due to real-world input drift (new user behaviors or unseen edge cases)."
   → `statements.problem`, `context.job`, `interpretations.problem`.

3. **When / where.** When the agent starts failing on real inputs nobody tested.
   [LYC] "Agent performance can often drop ~40% in a few weeks, and suddenly what worked in testing breaks in front of
   customers." [LYC] "When that happens, engineers are forced to dig through logs, collect failing examples, and manually
   tweak prompts rather than building core product features." → `context.circumstance`, `occasion: agent failure`.
   Author's choice: the window {5, WORKING_DAYS} and Frequency 3 to 5 working days out of 5; the launch says
   "continuously" and gives no count. The daily rhythm is confirmed only later, by a customer quote on [SITE]: "Every
   morning, I check our frontend logs -> backend logs -> Lemma logs, then pipe any issues straight into Claude".
   Prevalence `p_60_80` ("Most") is the author's: not every team's agent fails every week.

4. **Which people.** Engineers at US pre-seed to Series A startups with an agent serving customers.
   [LYC] "If you know a Head of AI/Eng or CTO at a pre-seed to Series A startup, we owe you lunch :)" → `context.segment`,
   `market: US` (author's choice: the founders are in the US batch and name no other market).

5. **Who pays.** The startup; its CTO or head of AI decides.
   [LYC] the ask above names the buyer, no payer or terms. → `persona.decision_maker: {role: founder}` (label
   "Startup CTOs and founders"; the id reads "The founder decides" in the engine's sentence). Buyer and payer tests
   "Nobody else" (at pre-seed the technical founder buys tools alone), with "The CEO" and "The security lead" listed:
   author's choice. Purchase friction's three items (a security review of sending traces out — tested; a check against
   the current observability tool; access to open pull requests) are the author's, drawn from [LYC]'s mechanism
   ("automatically open a PR in your codebase") and [YCP]'s "the silent failures your observability tools and evals
   miss". Commitment's step "connect one agent's traces for a trial": [LYC] "book a live demo on our website"; [WB]
   "Book a demo appointment to get started."; the trial on one agent is the author's next step after the demo.

6. **Mechanism.** Failed runs found in live traffic; the cause traced; a prompt fix opened as a pull request.
   [LYC] "Step 1: Lemma detects failed outcomes directly from live traffic, and it automatically identifies the exact
   cause in an agent chain." "Step 2: Lemma alerts you, and with one click, it runs targeted prompt optimizations to fix
   the failing behavior without any manual tracing or guesswork." "Step 3: We give you back an improved prompt and
   automatically open a PR in your codebase so your prompts can live where you want them." [LYC] "Agent tracing
   observability with live drift detection, regression alerts, and performance visibility across real user
   interactions." → `statements.solution`, `solution_mechanism`, Compatibility (every run already traced — tested;
   prompts in the repository; traces may leave the company) and Adoption friction (review and merge the prompt changes
   it opens — tested; add its tracing to the agent's code). Relative advantage: [LYC] "resolve production drifts in
   minutes instead of days" (easier_recovery) and "cut manual prompt iteration by 90%" (shorter_time); wording the
   author's.

7. **Price and cost.** No price is public at launch or since; the cost is a rate of failing runs.
   [LYC] asks for demos and introductions and names no price; [WB] "Book a demo appointment to get started."; [PRC] 404.
   → `commercial.price` AMOUNT_PERIOD $300 to $600 per agent a month: **the operator's reading**, not a source. The
   unit is the cost's (a chain price follows the cost's unit and period); the amount is the author's, a sum a CTO can
   approve alone that sits well under one engineer-week ([BLS]). `statements.commercial` carries the same reading.
   Existing sacrifice, RATE 10% to 40% of the agent's runs in production per agent a month, lossPhrase "Runs that fail in
   front of customers before anyone notices": the top is [LYC]'s "~40%", read as a share of runs (the launch says
   "performance"); the low end is the author's. Ability to pay is read `budget` by the engine (a percent of runs never
   compares with dollars), so the six founders answer the registry's budget question.

8. **Occasions.** The stories are scripted from these public accounts; no respondent is a real person.
   [LYC] "dig through logs, collect failing examples, and manually tweak prompts". [YCP] "We catch the silent failures
   your observability tools and evals miss (think bad tool calls, lost context, and infinite loops) before your users
   find them." (today's page, later than launch). [SITE] (customer, later) "almost immediately it flagged an issue that
   had gone unnoticed in prod for 20+ days".

## Respondents → the public account each is based on

AI engineers (PRIMARY link, Parts 1 and 2):
- Priya Venkataraman → [LYC] "what worked in testing breaks in front of customers"; the refund window from [SITE]'s demo incident ("P0 — promising refunds outside 30-day policy", later); the rest the author's.
- Mateo Fernández → [YCP] "infinite loops" and "bad tool calls" (later page); the bill spike the author's.
- Aisha Bello → author's invention, filling a gap: a team whose own eval suite catches regressions before they ship (against on Importance), so the problem is not a chorus.
- Jonah Feldman → [LYC] "collect failing examples, and manually tweak prompts"; [YCP] "lost context".
- Mei-Ling Zhou → author's invention, filling a gap: a chipped (rather_not_say) story, GUESSED by code.
- Kwabena Asare → author's invention, filling a gap: a vague, habitual story with no one occasion (GUESSED; Frequency `cant_recall`).
- Sofia Marchetti → author's invention: a gate No (her team's agent not yet live that week).
- Ravi Shankar → author's invention: a gate No (on leave).
- Daniel Kim → [SITE]'s demo failure mode ("the agent invents placeholder identifiers instead of asking"; "Every one returned success, so nothing surfaced in error monitoring.", later); he will not merge machine-written prompt changes (Adoption friction probably not).
- Elena Petrova → [LYC] the founders' healthcare background (Tandem); author's invention: runs only sampled and patient details stripped, so the tested condition fails for her (Compatibility only with help).
- Tyrone Jackson → author's invention, filling a gap: latency and cost, not wrong answers, are his week's problem (against on Importance).
- Hannah Goldberg → [LYC] "new user behaviors or unseen edge cases"; the language mix-up the author's.
- Omar Haddad → [P2] "many existing agent monitoring systems depend heavily on developers deciding beforehand what they want to measure. This can include configuring specific judges, traces, evaluation criteria, alerts or known failure conditions." — a team whose own judges catch the known failures (Current solution mostly works).
- Lucía Romero → [LYC] the manual prompt loop; [SITE]'s "Agents can look like they're working even when they've failed." (later).

Startup CTOs and founders (COMMERCIAL_B2B link, Part 3 only; no story by rule). Their picks are the author's, shaped by:
- Nathan Cole → [LYC] the ask to "a Head of AI/Eng or CTO at a pre-seed to Series A startup"; pays below the founder's band per agent (several small agents; the per-agent price adds up), though he would start the trial.
- Farah Siddiqui → author's invention: prices it below the band against the observability tool she already pays for, and wants a week on staging first (Commitment yes after trying).
- Wei Zhang → [SITE] (customer, later) "we switched over from raindrop a while back": a buyer who already pays for an observability tool and prices this below it.
- Isabel Duarte → [SITE] (customer, later) "it flagged an issue that had gone unnoticed in prod for 20+ days": a buyer who would pay above the band (beyond), with the CEO agreeing.
- Marcus Oyelaran → author's invention, filling a gap: a low-volume agent read by hand, so Nothing as the cost and would not pay.
- Chloe Bennett → [P2] agents "in workflows where failures have financial, operational or customer-facing consequences"; author's invention: a security lead who must clear any vendor seeing customer conversations, and a buyer who cannot say the cost or the price (both escapes).

The split (1 of the 5 founders who name a rung at $300 or above, the other four below it -- made harsher on
2026-10-22 so the price fails; 3 of 5 cost boxes at 10% or more) is the author's
reading of a crowded tooling market ([P2] "The emerging AI observability market includes tools for tracing model calls,
measuring latency, monitoring token usage, evaluating model responses and reviewing agent behavior.") against the
launch's claims. No respondent carries the name of a customer, commenter or founder in the sources.

## Status today

Same idea, re-led. The problem is unchanged (agents fail in production without anyone noticing); the lead product moved
from "Continuous Learning" and automated prompt optimization ([LYC], [WB]) to monitoring: [SITE] "Lemma | Production
monitoring for AI agents"; "Lemma audits every trace against your agent's instructions and groups recurring failures
into issues."; "Pull context into your coding agent to resolve it without context-switching." Raised $2.3 million
pre-seed ([P2], 2026-08-19). Price today: none public ([PRC] 404; [SITE] "Book a demo").

## Could not be sourced

- **Any price, at any time.** The founder's $300 to $600 per agent a month is the operator's reading (item 7), recorded
  as such in the entry's header and in `statements.commercial`. A run that reads the price line reads the author's
  number, not Lemma's.
- **A share of runs.** [LYC]'s 40 is a fall in "performance", not a share of failing runs; the RATE reading and its low
  end of 10 are the author's (header).
- **A buyer title in practice, the approvers and the purchase steps.** Only the launch ask names the buyer; the CEO and
  security lead, the three Purchase friction items and the trial step are the author's.
- **An engineer's hour.** [BLS]'s software developers' median stands in; a RATE cost does not use it.
- **The daily rhythm at launch.** The launch says "continuously"; the morning-check quote is today's site.
- **A Launch HN thread or first-person engineer accounts from the launch era.** None found; the customer quotes on
  [SITE] are vendor-curated and later than launch.

founder.order_why: The flow moves the way I'd pitch Lemma to a CTO: who the engineer is and where, the agent drifting in production, our trace-to-PR fix, then who buys, what it costs, what slows a purchase and the first step, and only then who runs the interviews.

screens.why2: "Startup CTO", "agree" and "buy" are words I use every day, and the "Nobody is an answer" hint makes the at-pre-seed case easy to say.
screens.why3: I sell to pre-seed to Series A CTOs and know who gets pulled in: the CEO on spend and a security lead once traces leave the company.
screens.why4: It's a free-text box with one escape chip, and "Leave this out of the study" fits a founder who doesn't want to test the approval chain.
screens.why5: My belief is that the CTO buys alone, which is what Keel wrote, but I typed "The CEO; The security lead" and the screen doesn't show that those are the alternatives to test, so it reads as if Keel dropped my two names.
screens.instead: Besides the startup CTO, who else would have to agree before buying? (Nobody else / The CEO / The security lead / Someone else)

screens.why1: Right after I named who else might have to agree, a check of the cast list before the commercial questions go out is where I'd expect it.
screens.why2: AI engineer, startup CTO, CEO and security lead are the plain titles at a pre-seed to Series A startup, and the intro is clear on first read.
screens.why3: I know exactly who touches a tooling purchase at the startups I sell to, so I can check this list from my own deals.
screens.why4: The first two rows carry a role tag but the CEO and the security lead carry none, so I can't tell whether Keel has them as approvers, as people the respondents get asked about, or as nobody, which sits oddly beside the belief.
screens.why5: The belief keeps my answer (the CTO decides, nobody else has to agree), but listing the CEO and the security lead under 'The people involved' with no tag drifts toward saying they are part of the buy, when I only put them up as names for buyers to pick against 'Nobody else'.
screens.instead: The people involved: AI engineer · has the problem; Startup CTO · decides to buy; The CEO · asked about, not needed; The security lead · asked about, not needed

screens.why1: Right after Keel checked who else must agree, choosing which of those approver beliefs to test is the obvious next step.
screens.why2: The three options are plain, but 'Pick the one role; nothing is reworded here' is Keel's own talk and takes a second read, especially since 'Nobody else' isn't a role.
screens.why3: Whether a pre-seed CTO buys dev tooling alone is exactly what I believe and see in my buyers, so I can pick without guessing.
screens.why4: The CEO, the security lead and nobody else are exactly the approvers I named, distinct and complete, with no stray option.
screens.why5: My 'nobody else' belief is kept, but the bar asks about 'the last time they bought agents that learn from their mistakes', a category no CTO has bought; what they buy is agent monitoring or observability tooling, so the test drifts from my product.
screens.instead: Which one do you want to test? The CEO / The security lead / Nobody else — the bar: Holds if at least 2 in 3 startup CTOs say nobody else had to agree the last time they bought a tool to monitor or debug their AI agent in production.

screens.why1: Right after naming who else must agree, asking what could stall the deal is the obvious next step in how it sells, and I have real answers: security, our current observability tool, and repo access.
screens.why2: Approvals, reviews, procurement and switching are plain words to a founder selling dev tools to startup CTOs, and the 25-word cap is clear.
screens.why3: I sell to these CTOs and know exactly what holds a deal up: sending traces out, overlap with the observability tool they already pay for, and letting a vendor open PRs.
screens.why4: It is a free-text box with a single 'Leave this out of the study' escape, which fits a question a founder might choose not to test.
screens.why5: My three frictions are kept as typed, but the belief Keel wrote tests only the security review and adds an 'about 3 weeks' threshold I never gave, which is long for a pre-seed CTO.

screens.why1: This screen comes right after I named what could slow a purchase, so checking Keel's list of what has to happen first is the obvious next step.
screens.why2: Traces, an observability tool and pull requests are everyday words to a startup CTO running an agent, and each row reads on first pass.
screens.why3: A CTO buying dev tooling knows whether traces can leave the company, what they already pay for observability, and whether a vendor bot may open PRs.
screens.why4: My three gates are there and distinct, but Keel's added 'A signed vendor agreement' is a generic enterprise step that rarely gates a pre-seed CTO buying alone, and it sits close to the security review.
screens.why5: The three gates I typed are kept word for word, the belief tests the one I care most about (traces leaving the company), and nothing leaks to a respondent.
screens.instead: Keep my three rows and drop 'A signed vendor agreement'; belief: 'Most startup CTOs would clear a security review of sending traces out within about a week, or not need it.'

screens.why1: Right after I named and checked the purchase blockers, it makes sense to pick the one I most fear and put my own time on it before strangers are asked.
screens.why2: Traces, observability tool and PRs are plain to me, but 'how long would this step take before it went through' reads twice, since 'it' could be the step or the purchase, and the time hint shows above the list before I've picked anything.
screens.why3: I know what a security review of sending traces to a vendor costs a seed-stage team in calendar time, so I can give my own estimate.
screens.why4: My three blockers are there in my words; the added 'signed vendor agreement' is distinct and plausible; the days, weeks and months menu covers the range.
screens.why5: The belief, 'Most startup CTOs would get through a security review of sending traces out within about 3 weeks, or not need it', is exactly my pick and my 3 weeks, and nothing of Lemma leaks.
screens.instead: Which step do you want to test? The buyer will be asked: if you bought it, how long would this step hold up the purchase? (Pick one, then give your own estimate in days, weeks or months.)

screens.why1: After who decides, what it costs and what slows a purchase, asking what first real step I'd want the CTO to take is the natural close of the sales section.
screens.why2: "First real step" with the hint about time, data, money or a signature is plain to a founder who sells developer tools through demos and trials.
screens.why3: I know exactly what I ask for after a demo: hook one agent's traces up so Lemma can show failures on real traffic.
screens.why4: It's a free-text box with a 25-word cap that fits a one-line step, and "Leave this out of the study" is the right escape for a founder who has no step to test.
screens.why5: The belief keeps my step word for word ("connect one agent's traces for a trial") and only adds the startup CTO and "in most cases", which is what I meant.

screens.why1: Right after I named the first step, it makes sense to check how Keel will put that step to strangers before Step 4 closes.
screens.why2: "Connect one agent's traces for a trial" is how I'd say it myself; traces and a trial are everyday words to a startup CTO running an LLM agent.
screens.why3: Whether a CTO would wire one agent's traces into a new tool is exactly what my buyers decide, and I can judge it from the demos I run.
screens.why4: The intro promises my step in under 9 words, but the screen only shows the full belief sentence, so I can't see the short wording strangers will actually hear; the bar's 'probably not or no' scale itself is fine.
screens.why5: The meaning is mine, but 'now' drifts a little: my step comes after a booked demo, and a CTO asked cold about 'now' with an unknown vendor will lean toward no on the security review alone.
screens.instead: Strangers hear: "Connect one agent's traces for a free trial." Keel will test: In most cases the startup CTO would connect one agent's traces for a trial after a demo.

screens.why1: Right after I named the first real step, asking whether to put a trial offer in front of the engineers who answer is the obvious next decision before the study goes out.
screens.why2: "Offer a pilot?" with "Yes, ask them / No pilot" is plain to a founder selling dev tooling, and the hint says exactly what the respondent sees and where I see the yeses.
screens.why3: Whether I want design partners from this study is my own call; post-launch I am actively looking for teams to work with.
screens.why4: Yes or no is the whole choice here, the two options are distinct, and no escape is needed for a founder's own decision.
screens.why5: The line respondents get is a generic "Would you try this for real?" rather than my step, "connect one agent's traces for a trial", so the ask an AI engineer sees drifts from the concrete trial I set on the screen before.
screens.instead: Offer a pilot? People who say yes get a line at the end: "Would you connect one agent's traces for a trial? Leave your email." (Yes, ask them / No pilot)

screens.why1: Picking who asks the questions fits right before the study goes out, after the pilot offer and before launch, and nothing earlier asked it.
screens.why2: The question is plain, but the hint packs video, voice, typing, a 400-credit charge, recording 'once' and text-message delivery into one block, and it says voice where the interviewer is on video, so I'd read it twice to know whether I'm picking a face or a voice.
screens.why3: I can choose by tapping each sample and hearing which one my engineers would sit through.
screens.why4: Two named interviewers with 5-second previews, a default already picked, and the same cost either way is a complete and distinct choice.
screens.why5: It names my respondents as AI engineers, as I typed, and shows nothing of Lemma or my buyer roles to the people answering.
screens.instead: Who should ask AI engineers your questions? (Keel's on-video interviewer; every question is also on screen to type or tap. Same 400 credits either way.) Options: Daphne ▶ 5 s · Saskia ▶ 5 s

screens.why1: Once the study is built and the interview style chosen, deciding who receives the link is the obvious last step before sending.
screens.why2: Plain words for a founder who would DM engineers from Tandem and Chipstack circles, though 'Contacts page' assumes I know Keel's other screen.
screens.why3: I know whether I am sending to engineers I know by name or posting in a Slack or Discord where AI engineers already hang out.

screens.why_b1: The verdict 'Not holding up' sits under the title with the deciding number beside it: 'Price: 1 of 5 at $300 or more per agent a month'.
screens.why_b2: Most cards say what is counted, out of how many and where the bar is (3 of 5, bar 4 of 5, 1 short), but Ability to pay's '1 of 5 named your price or more · 5 needed' needs a second look, and the 5-versus-6 bases aren't explained.
screens.why_b3: Buyer and payer, Purchase friction and Commitment carry my belief lines word for word, and the other cards read as the beliefs I checked on the way in.
screens.why_b4: The statement under the verdict only explains who answered, and 'they value it below your price' hints at the problem, but nothing says what to do, such as rethinking the per-agent price or retesting with a lower band.
screens.why_b5: n=6 is visible and Ability to pay is honestly 'Too few to call', but three cards are called 'Holding up' at exactly 4 of 6 or 2 of 6 with no word that six people is a thin base.
screens.instead: Not holding up on price: only 1 of 5 CTOs would pay $300+ per agent a month. Buyer, friction and trial only just clear their bars, from 6 people. Try a lower or per-team price before anything else.

screens.why_b1: The count beside the verdict is clear (3 of 5, bar 4 of 5, 1 short), but the status word 'People disagree a split' never says plainly that my belief did not hold, so I have to work out the verdict from the number.
screens.why_b2: The axis unit and the 3-for, 2-against strip read quickly, but 'bar 4 of 5 (at least 2 in 3)' needs a second look to see why two-thirds of 5 becomes 4, and the 'You said' line is printed twice.
screens.why_b3: Existing sacrifice and the 10% to 40% of runs failing in front of customers before anyone notices are my own words and range.
screens.why_b4: The So line repeats the count and points me to the Price card, but it never says what a 3-of-5 split on lost runs means for my pitch, such as leading with the teams losing 10% or more.
screens.why_b5: n stays visible (6 answered, 5 counted), Marcus's zero and Chloe's can't-recall are explained, and 'a small group: a lean, not a call' keeps it from overstating.

screens.why_b4: It rightly sends me back to price ('Price decides this stage'), but 'waits until at least 5 name your price' means all five CTOs I asked, which won't happen at this price, so it tells me to wait rather than what to change.
screens.why_b5: n stays visible, the small group is called out as 'a lean, not a call', and Isabel's single budget-line answer is never presented as support for the belief.

screens.why_b1: The verdict 'Holding up' sits right beside its deciding number, 4 of 6 could sign alone against a bar of 4 of 6, at the bar.

screens.why_b4: "Book them into it" is concrete: I can put Nathan, Farah, Wei and Isabel on a one-agent trace trial this week.

screens.why_b1: Each box opens on its verdict (Price not holding up, Buyer and payer holding up) with the deciding count beside it: 1 of 5 at $300 or more against a bar of 4, and 4 of 6 could sign alone at a bar of 4.
screens.why_b3: The dimension names and belief lines are the ones I checked: the CTO decides alone, and my $300 to $600 per agent a month reading, in my own unit.
screens.why_b4: The quotes point the way (price against the tracing bill, price per team not per agent, prove it fixes rather than flags, show the CEO one miss and tell security where traces live), but the screen never says what this means for the idea; the reader has to work it out.
screens.why_b5: The counts stay visible and 'at the bar' is said, but a 'Holding up' resting on exactly 4 of 6 never says the sample is too small to lean on, and the 'On their own' label hides that Marcus said there is nothing to pay for yet.
screens.why_b6: I did not type these: buyers anchor my price to their whole observability bill, per-agent pricing breaks for teams with several small agents, flagging alone is not worth paying for, the CEO wants one failure our evals missed, and security wants to know where traces are stored.
screens.instead: Price fails because buyers set it against their tracing bill and per-agent pricing adds up, so try a per-team price under that bill and lead with fixes, not flags; Buyer and payer holds only at the bar on 6, so bring one caught failure for the CEO and a trace-storage answer for security.

screens.why1: The idea card belongs before price on my link, but it opens cold as the very first screen with no question about whether my agent in production has broken on real traffic, so I meet a product pitch before anything about my situation.
screens.why2: Live traffic, agent chain, eval sets, tracing, drift alerts and pull request are all my everyday words, but 'a failure alert and fix' is a clumsy label that I had to read twice to work out what kind of thing Lemma is.
screens.why3: Agents failing on customer inputs we never tested, and chasing the cause through traces, is exactly what my team deals with, so I can judge this from my own work.
screens.why4: A card to read, with no options.
screens.why5: Nothing leaks that shouldn't, but the belief line only restates that a better prompt lands in the PR, which drifts from what the idea is for: keeping the agent doing what customers need as traffic changes.
screens.why6: Heard once, it is a lot to hold: three feature-dense sentences, a 20-plus-word middle sentence, and a three-item tool list at the end, with nothing to say it can't be spoken but heavy for one hearing.
screens.instead: Imagine Lemma, a tool that catches your agent failing on real customer traffic and drafts the fix. It finds which step in the agent caused the failure, alerts your engineers, and with one click opens a pull request with an improved prompt. The people building it believe it would fix production failures before customers keep hitting them.

screens.why1: Right after the idea card, asking how often my agent quietly failed customers last month is the obvious way to measure what the problem costs me now.
screens.why2: 'Runs in production' is my language, but 'failed in front of customers before anyone noticed' is fuzzy: does a wrong-but-plausible answer count as failed, and noticed by whom, us or the customer?
screens.why3: By definition I only know about the failures we eventually caught, usually from a customer complaint, so a share of all runs would be a guess and not something I can look up.
screens.why4: The number box is fine, but 'None' just duplicates typing 0 and adds a second escape beside 'I can't recall', which breaks the one-escape rule.
screens.why5: Nothing of the founder's product leaks; it reads as a plain question about my own agent's failures.
screens.why6: The question says once, but the tail 'a percent of runs in production last month, or a low and a high; none is 0' is a mouthful of instructions on top of two escapes.
screens.instead: Last month, how many times did a customer get a wrong answer from your agent that you only found out about afterwards? (a number box; escape: I can't recall)

screens.why1: Right after the idea and the question on how often my agents fail in front of customers, asking what it's worth to me is the obvious next step for the person who signs for the tool.
screens.why2: A monthly price per agent is how I already think about tooling for our agents, so I can answer it on first read.
screens.why3: I choose and pay for our eng tools and know roughly what I'd spend across our handful of small agents, so I can name a band.
screens.why4: The bands don't overlap, they cover everything from almost nothing to a lot, 'I wouldn't pay for this' is there, and 'I can't say' fits as the escape; with several small agents I'd probably land under $100, but that option exists.
screens.why5: Only the idea card as shown says what Lemma is, and per agent per month is a plain pricing unit, not the founder's own language reaching me.
screens.why6: The two-step reading of the bands is easy to hold, but 'Or say you can't say' trips when heard and sounds like a riddle rather than a way out.
screens.instead: What would Lemma be worth to you a month, per agent? Under $300; $300 to under $500; $500 or more; or you wouldn't pay for this. Or say 'I can't say'.

screens.why1: Right after I put a price on it, asking what would push that number up is the obvious next question and doesn't repeat anything I've already said.
screens.why2: Plain words I'd use myself, and I can answer it straight away, though the echo leaves out 'a month, per agent', so I have to remember that's what the range meant.
screens.why3: I know exactly what would make it worth more to me, like cutting the failures customers see or pricing that doesn't stack up across several small agents, so this is my own call to make.
screens.why4: It's a box to type in, with no options to judge.
screens.why5: It just plays back my own price band and uses the name from the idea card, so nothing new about the founder's plan reaches me.
screens.why6: Two short sentences, and the range says well aloud as 'a hundred to under three hundred dollars', with no parenthesis, slash or list to hold.
screens.instead: You put Lemma at $100 to under $300 a month per agent. What would make it worth more to you?

screens.why1: After asking who signs off on the money, it makes sense to ask what else would hold the purchase up, and for a tool that ships our agent traces to someone else, security is the obvious hurdle.
screens.why2: Traces and security review are my everyday words, but 'sending traces out' is clunky; I'd say 'sending our traces to a third party' or 'to their servers'.
screens.why3: I'm the one who would run or skip that review, and I know whether a customer contract or a SOC 2 commitment would force one, so I can answer from my own shop.
screens.why4: The options mostly work and 'It wouldn't be needed' covers a lot of seed-stage teams, but '3 weeks to 3 months' and '3 to 6 months' both include 3 months, and the one-week band between 2 and 3 weeks sits oddly next to a ten-week one.
screens.why5: The idea card already said Lemma reads our production traces, so asking about a review of sending them out reveals nothing new and keeps the founder's meaning.
screens.why6: Heard once it works: one short question, three time bands plus 'it wouldn't be needed', one escape, and a quick either-or follow-up I can answer right away.
screens.instead: If you bought Lemma, how long would a security review of sending your traces to them take? Under 2 weeks · 2 to under 3 weeks · 3 weeks to under 3 months · 3 to 6 months · Over 6 months · It wouldn't be needed

screens.why1: After the price, the sign-off and the security review, asking whether I'd actually wire up an agent for a trial is the obvious last step.
screens.why2: Connecting an agent's traces for a trial is how I'd talk about trying an observability tool, so I get it on first read.
screens.why3: I make this call myself and know whether I'd plug one of our agents into a new tool this week.
screens.why4: The scale leans negative: there's a 'Probably not' but no 'Probably yes', so my real answer, likely yes pending the security review, has nowhere honest to go.
screens.why5: It stays on the founder's ask, a trial on one agent's traces, and nothing leaks beyond the idea card I was already shown.
screens.why6: One short question with three options that are easy to hold when heard, and no escape is needed on a commitment item.
screens.instead: If it were ready today, would you connect one agent's traces for a trial, or not? Yes, I'd connect one · Probably yes · Probably not · No
